overview: Row Level Security (RLS) in Databricks restricts which rows a user can see in a table by attaching a row-filter function to the table through Unity Catalog.

A row filter is a user-defined function (UDF) registered in Unity Catalog that returns a boolean per row; Unity Catalog automatically applies it as a predicate on every query against the protected table.
RLS is typically combined with column masks and group membership (often via mapping tables) to deliver fine-grained, centrally governed access control without duplicating data into multiple views.
learningObjectives: Understand how Unity Catalog row-filter functions restrict visible rows based on the querying user's identity or group membership.
Learn to create, apply, and combine ROW FILTER and column masks on a table, including using mapping tables for multi-tenant isolation.
Compare row-filter-based RLS against the traditional view-based RLS pattern and reason about performance and governance trade-offs.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Row Level Security in Databricks is a Unity Catalog governance feature that associates a SQL user-defined function (the row filter) with a table; the function is evaluated as a WHERE predicate for every read, returning TRUE for rows the current principal is permitted to see and FALSE otherwise. The filter can reference the runtime identity functions current_user(), is_account_group_member(), and is_member(), as well as columns of the row, enabling attribute-based and group-based access control enforced transparently at query time.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine a single shared spreadsheet of all sales records, but when each regional manager opens it they only ever see the rows for their own region. Row Level Security is the rule that quietly hides the rows you are not allowed to see, no matter how you query the table. You write one small function that says 'show this row only if it matches the user', attach it to the table once, and Databricks enforces it for everyone automatically.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Before Unity Catalog, Databricks practitioners implemented RLS by creating secured views with WHERE clauses on current_user() and revoking access to base tables, or by using dynamic view functions in Hive Metastore. Databricks introduced Unity Catalog as a unified governance layer, and in 2023 added native row filters and column masks (GA in late 2023) so that fine-grained access control could be declared directly on tables and inherited consistently across SQL warehouses and clusters, removing the need to manage proliferating secured views.

whyItMatters.business: Enables a single governed copy of sensitive data (PII, financial, multi-tenant) to safely serve many audiences, satisfying regulations like GDPR, HIPAA, and SOC 2 while reducing data duplication and the risk of accidental exposure.
whyItMatters.engineering: Centralizes access logic in one reusable function rather than scattering WHERE clauses across dozens of views or downstream queries, dramatically lowering maintenance burden and the chance of an inconsistent or leaky policy.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because the filter is applied at the catalog level, it scales to thousands of tables and users without creating thousands of views; new consumers inherit the policy automatically with no schema changes.
whyItMatters.cost: Avoids storing and refreshing multiple physically partitioned copies of data per tenant or region, cutting storage and pipeline compute, though it adds a small per-query predicate evaluation cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: A single source of truth for both data and access policy reduces drift; auditors and engineers can inspect one function to know exactly who can see what, improving trust and reducing security incidents.

coreComponents.name: Row Filter Function
coreComponents.definition: A Unity Catalog SQL UDF that takes one or more column values as parameters and returns a BOOLEAN indicating whether the current principal may see the row.
coreComponents.purpose: To encapsulate the row-visibility logic in a single reusable, governable object.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Evaluate identity functions (current_user, is_account_group_member) and/or join against mapping tables to decide TRUE/FALSE per row.
coreComponents.examples: CREATE FUNCTION region_filter(region STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN RETURN is_account_group_member('admins') OR region = current_user_region()

coreComponents.name: Table Row-Filter Binding
coreComponents.definition: The association created with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER fn ON (col) that attaches a filter function to specific columns of a table.
coreComponents.purpose: To declare that Unity Catalog must apply the filter predicate on every query of the table.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Map table columns to the filter function's parameters and ensure the predicate is injected into all read paths.
coreComponents.examples: ALTER TABLE sales SET ROW FILTER catalog.sec.region_filter ON (region);

coreComponents.name: Mapping Table
coreComponents.definition: A governance table that maps principals or groups to the data values (regions, tenant_ids, departments) they are allowed to access.
coreComponents.purpose: To externalize the user-to-data entitlement relationship so policies can change by editing data rather than code.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Store rows like (user_email, allowed_tenant_id) and be joined inside the row-filter function to resolve permissions.
coreComponents.examples: user_access(user_email STRING, tenant_id STRING) joined inside the filter on current_user()

internalWorking: When a query is submitted against a table that has a row filter bound, the Unity Catalog query analyzer rewrites the logical plan to wrap the table scan with the filter function applied as a predicate, passing the bound columns as arguments.

The filter function is evaluated using the security context of the querying principal, so identity functions such as current_user() and is_account_group_member('grp') resolve to that principal's identity and group memberships at query time.

If the function returns FALSE for a row, that row is eliminated before any downstream operators (joins, aggregations, projections) see it; column masks, if present, are then applied to the surviving rows' protected columns.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: User Query -> Unity Catalog Authorization -> Plan Rewrite (inject row filter predicate + column masks) -> Filtered Table Scan -> Downstream Operators -> Result (only permitted rows/columns)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Analyst alice@corp.com runs SELECT * FROM sales where the table has region_filter bound on the region column.
2. Unity Catalog rewrites the plan to SELECT * FROM sales WHERE region_filter(region), evaluated as alice.
3. region_filter checks is_account_group_member('sales_admin') (false for alice) then joins user_access to find alice's allowed regions ('EMEA').
4. Rows where region = 'EMEA' return TRUE and pass through; rows for 'NA' and 'APAC' return FALSE and are dropped before alice ever sees them, so her result contains only EMEA rows.

keyTerminology.meaning: A Unity Catalog function applied to a table that returns a boolean per row, deciding whether the current principal can see that row.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the core enforcement mechanism for RLS, applied transparently to every query.

keyTerminology.meaning: A Unity Catalog function applied to a column that transforms or redacts the column value (e.g., showing only last 4 digits) based on the principal.
keyTerminology.importance: Complements row filters to provide cell-level security; together they give full fine-grained access control.

keyTerminology.meaning: A built-in function returning TRUE if the current principal belongs to the named account-level group in Unity Catalog.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the recommended, identity-provider-synced way to implement group-based RLS rather than the workspace-local is_member().

importantConcepts.explanation: Filters can branch on is_account_group_member('grp') for coarse role checks (e.g., admins see all rows) and fall back to current_user() lookups or mapping-table joins for per-user entitlements. Group membership is preferred because it is centrally managed via the identity provider and avoids hardcoding emails.

importantConcepts.concept: Combining row filters with column masks
importantConcepts.explanation: A table can have at most one row filter but many column masks. The row filter decides which rows survive; column masks then redact sensitive columns on those surviving rows. This separation lets you, for example, let users see all rows of their tenant (row filter) but still mask SSNs unless they are in the 'pii_readers' group (column mask).

variationsAndTypes: **Static/group-based RLS:** Filter branches purely on group membership (admins see all, others see a fixed subset). Simple and fast.
**Mapping-table RLS:** Filter joins a governance table mapping users/groups to permitted values, enabling data-driven, multi-tenant entitlements without code changes.
**View-based RLS (legacy):** A secured view embeds the WHERE clause and base tables are hidden; used when row filters are unavailable or when reshaping schema is also required.
advantages: **Centralized policy:** One function governs row visibility across all queries and compute, eliminating scattered WHERE clauses.
**Single source of truth:** Data is stored once; no duplicated per-tenant tables or sprawling views.
**Automatic inheritance:** New consumers and tools (BI, notebooks, SQL warehouses) get the policy transparently with no extra work.
**Composable:** Combines cleanly with column masks for true cell-level governance, all auditable in Unity Catalog.
disadvantages: **Query overhead:** The filter predicate (especially with mapping-table joins) adds evaluation cost to every query and can defeat some pruning if poorly designed.
**One filter per table:** Complex multi-dimensional rules must be packed into a single function, which can grow hard to read.
**Requires Unity Catalog:** Not available in the legacy Hive Metastore; tables must be UC-managed/external under a metastore.
**Debugging complexity:** Because filtering is implicit, users seeing 'missing' rows may be confused, and engineers must reason about the rewritten plan.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use row-filter RLS when you have a single governed table serving many audiences (multi-tenant SaaS, regional teams, PII-bearing analytics) and want centrally managed, auditable, automatically inherited policies under Unity Catalog.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid (or prefer views/physical partitioning) when not on Unity Catalog, when access logic also requires reshaping columns/joins better expressed as a view, or when extreme low-latency queries cannot tolerate any predicate overhead and tenants can instead be physically isolated.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of a corporate building with one master floor plan but smart ID badges. Every employee walks the same hallways, but the doors that open depend on the badge they tap. RLS is the badge reader on every door: the building (the table) is shared, yet each person only ever reaches the rooms (rows) their badge (identity/group) permits, and you change access by updating the badge system once, not by rebuilding the building.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Row filters slow queries down catastrophically and should be avoided for big tables.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A well-written filter that branches on group membership and references partition/clustering columns adds minimal overhead and still allows file pruning; the cost is usually small relative to the scan and far cheaper than maintaining duplicated data.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can have multiple row filters on one table to express different rules.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unity Catalog allows only one row filter per table. Multiple conditions must be combined inside the single filter function using AND/OR logic; you can, however, attach many column masks.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Row filters scale to many tables and users because policy lives in reusable functions and mapping tables; for very large mapping tables, broadcast-friendly sizing and indexing-by-clustering of the protected table keep predicate evaluation efficient.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Centralizing access in one function reduces policy drift and accidental leaks; changes are versioned and audited in Unity Catalog, and the same enforcement applies identically across all compute.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because the filter is metadata bound to the table, it survives cluster restarts and is reapplied automatically; there is no per-session state to lose, so failover does not weaken enforcement.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Use Unity Catalog system tables (system.access.audit) and query history to monitor who queried protected tables, and review function definitions and bindings via INFORMATION_SCHEMA to detect unauthorized changes.
productionConsiderations.security: RLS is a primary security control: it must run with least privilege, filter functions should default to denying rows (return FALSE) on unknown principals, and ownership of the function/mapping table must be tightly restricted so consumers cannot bypass or alter the policy.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Avoids duplicate-copy storage and redundant ETL per tenant; keep mapping tables small and the protected table well-clustered on filter columns so the predicate prunes files rather than forcing full scans.
productionConsiderations.performance: Reference partition or liquid-clustering columns inside the filter so Databricks can prune data files; prefer cheap is_account_group_member checks before expensive mapping-table joins, and keep mapping tables broadcastable.

codeExamples.title: Group-based row filter with admin bypass
codeExamples.overview: Create a Unity Catalog row-filter function that lets members of the sales_admin group see all rows while restricting everyone else to their own region, then bind it to the sales table.
codeExamples.code:
-- 1. Create the row-filter function (returns TRUE for rows the caller may see)
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION secure.access.region_filter(region STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN
  is_account_group_member('sales_admin')
  OR region = (
    SELECT allowed_region
    FROM secure.access.user_region_map
    WHERE user_email = current_user()
  );

-- 2. Bind the filter to the table, mapping the 'region' column to the function arg
ALTER TABLE prod.sales.transactions
SET ROW FILTER secure.access.region_filter ON (region);

-- 3. Any subsequent query is transparently filtered
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM prod.sales.transactions
GROUP BY region;
codeExamples.breakdown: The function returns a boolean per row. is_account_group_member checks the account-level group first (cheap short-circuit) so admins bypass the restriction. Non-admins are matched against a mapping table keyed on current_user(). ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER binds the function and maps the table's region column to the function parameter, after which every read is rewritten to apply the predicate.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A sales_admin sees revenue for all regions; a regular analyst's GROUP BY returns only their single allowed region's revenue, with other regions silently excluded.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting that only one row filter is allowed per table; referencing a column name in ON(...) that does not match the function parameter order; the function defaulting to NULL (treated as not TRUE) when current_user() is absent from the mapping table, unexpectedly hiding all rows.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Put the cheap is_account_group_member check first to short-circuit for admins; keep user_region_map small so it broadcasts; cluster the transactions table on region so the predicate enables file pruning.

codeExamples.title: Multi-tenant mapping-table filter combined with a column mask
codeExamples.overview: Implement multi-tenant isolation where users see only their tenant's rows (row filter via a many-to-many mapping table) and also mask the email column for non-privileged users (column mask).
codeExamples.code:
-- Mapping table: a user may have access to multiple tenants
-- secure.access.tenant_acl(user_email STRING, tenant_id STRING)

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION secure.access.tenant_filter(tenant_id STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN
  is_account_group_member('platform_ops')
  OR EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM secure.access.tenant_acl a
    WHERE a.user_email = current_user()
      AND a.tenant_id = tenant_filter.tenant_id
  );

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION secure.access.mask_email(email STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN is_account_group_member('pii_readers') THEN email
  ELSE regexp_replace(email, '(^.).*(@.*$)', '$1***$2')
END;

ALTER TABLE prod.app.customers SET ROW FILTER secure.access.tenant_filter ON (tenant_id);
ALTER TABLE prod.app.customers ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK secure.access.mask_email;
codeExamples.breakdown: The row filter uses EXISTS against a many-to-many ACL so a single user can be entitled to several tenants; platform_ops bypasses for support. The column mask is a separate function attached to the email column: pii_readers see the raw value, everyone else sees a redacted form. Row filter runs first (drops non-tenant rows), then the mask redacts surviving rows.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A tenant user sees only rows for their entitled tenant_id(s) with emails masked to 'a***@domain.com'; a pii_readers member of platform_ops sees all tenants with full emails.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Qualifying the function parameter incorrectly inside EXISTS (use the function name prefix tenant_filter.tenant_id to disambiguate from the table column); attaching a mask to a column already used by another mask; forgetting that masks and filters require the function to be in a catalog the table can reference.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep the ACL clustered/small for broadcast joins; check group membership before the EXISTS subquery; ensure tenant_id is a clustering column so the row filter prunes files per tenant.

codeExamples.title: Inspecting and removing policies via PySpark / SQL
codeExamples.overview: Programmatically verify which row filters and masks are bound to a table and how to drop them, useful for CI/CD governance pipelines.
codeExamples.code:
# PySpark in a Databricks notebook
# Inspect bound row filters and column masks from INFORMATION_SCHEMA
filters = spark.sql("""
  SELECT table_name, filter_name, target_columns
  FROM prod.information_schema.row_filters
  WHERE table_schema = 'sales'
""")
filters.show(truncate=False)

masks = spark.sql("""
  SELECT table_name, column_name, mask_name
  FROM prod.information_schema.column_masks
  WHERE table_schema = 'app'
""")
masks.show(truncate=False)

# Remove a policy (e.g., during a controlled migration)
spark.sql("ALTER TABLE prod.sales.transactions DROP ROW FILTER")
spark.sql("ALTER TABLE prod.app.customers ALTER COLUMN email DROP MASK")
codeExamples.breakdown: Unity Catalog exposes row_filters and column_masks views in each catalog's information_schema, so governance code can audit bindings without parsing DDL. DROP ROW FILTER and DROP MASK detach the policy. Wrapping this in PySpark lets you run it inside CI/CD or scheduled compliance jobs.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The first two queries print the active filter and mask bindings; the ALTER statements detach them, after which queries return unfiltered/unmasked data (so dropping must be tightly access-controlled).
codeExamples.commonIssues: Running DROP without sufficient privileges (must own or have MANAGE on the table); assuming dropping a function also detaches it (you must DROP ROW FILTER first or the function drop fails while in use); querying information_schema in the wrong catalog.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Cache the audit results and diff against an expected-policy manifest in source control; alert if a table that should be protected has no row filter bound.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A B2B analytics SaaS stores all customers' event data in one Unity Catalog table to simplify pipelines, but each customer (tenant) must see only their own rows, internal support engineers must see all tenants for troubleshooting, and customer PII (email) must be masked from analysts who are not authorized PII readers.
endToEndExample.inputData: prod.app.events(event_id, tenant_id, user_email, event_type, ts, payload); a governance ACL secure.access.tenant_acl(user_email, tenant_id); account groups platform_support and pii_readers synced from the identity provider.
endToEndExample.architecture: Unity Catalog metastore over a Delta Lakehouse. One physical events table clustered on tenant_id. A row-filter function (tenant_filter) and a column-mask function (mask_email) are registered in secure.access and bound to the events table. SQL warehouses and notebooks all read through the same governed table.
processingSteps: 1. Create the ACL table and populate it from the entitlement system mapping each support/customer user to their tenant_id(s).
2. Create tenant_filter(tenant_id) returning TRUE for platform_support members or when an ACL row matches current_user().
3. Create mask_email(email) returning the raw email for pii_readers and a redacted value otherwise.
4. ALTER TABLE events SET ROW FILTER tenant_filter ON (tenant_id) and ALTER COLUMN user_email SET MASK mask_email.
5. Validate by querying as a customer user, a support user, and a pii_reader; confirm row visibility and masking match policy.
endToEndExample.output: A single governed events table where each tenant user sees only their rows with emails masked, support engineers see all tenants, and authorized PII readers see unmasked emails, all without any duplicated tables or per-tenant views.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track query history and system.access.audit for reads of events; periodically diff information_schema.row_filters/column_masks against the expected-policy manifest; alert if the filter is dropped or the ACL changes unexpectedly.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: The filter defaults to FALSE (deny) for users not present in the ACL, so an entitlement gap fails closed rather than leaking data; CI tests assert that a synthetic unauthorized user receives zero rows and a masked column.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Strong multi-tenant isolation and PII protection from a single source of truth, with policy changes made by editing the ACL data rather than rewriting queries, satisfying SOC 2 and contractual data-isolation requirements at minimal storage and maintenance cost.

industryUseCases.company: B2B SaaS platforms (e.g., multi-tenant analytics vendors)
industryUseCases.problem: Storing all tenants' data in shared tables for pipeline simplicity while contractually guaranteeing each customer sees only their own data.
industryUseCases.solution: A row-filter function joins a tenant ACL on current_user() and is bound to every shared table on the tenant_id column, with a support-group bypass for troubleshooting.
industryUseCases.benefits: Guaranteed tenant isolation from one governed copy, no per-tenant table sprawl, and entitlement changes made by editing data, supporting SOC 2 compliance.

industryUseCases.problem: Regional managers and analysts should see only their own region's sales or employee records, while corporate roles see everything.
industryUseCases.solution: A region/department row filter branches on is_account_group_member for HQ roles and otherwise matches the user against a region mapping table, combined with column masks on compensation fields.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, centrally governed regional access across all BI tools without maintaining dozens of regional views.

industryUseCases.problem: Analysts need population-level data but must be barred from records outside their care team or business unit and from raw identifiers unless authorized.
industryUseCases.solution: Row filters scope rows to the user's organizational unit while column masks redact SSNs, account numbers, and names except for privileged groups, all audited via Unity Catalog system tables.
industryUseCases.benefits: Enforces HIPAA/GLBA minimum-necessary access with auditable, centralized policy and no duplicated de-identified datasets.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Policies are reusable functions plus small mapping tables, so adding tables or users does not multiply objects. Keep ACL/mapping tables small enough to broadcast and cluster protected tables on filter columns; for very large entitlement sets, denormalize the ACL or precompute per-user allowed-value arrays to keep predicate evaluation cheap.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Filters and masks are table metadata in the metastore, so they are reapplied automatically after cluster or warehouse restarts and survive failover; there is no session-local enforcement that could be lost, ensuring the policy is never accidentally bypassed during recovery.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Because enforcement lives in Unity Catalog and is identical across all SQL warehouses and clusters in the metastore region, any available compute enforces the same policy; the metastore's managed availability backs the control plane.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Treat filter/mask function DDL, bindings, and mapping-table contents as governed code: store DDL in source control and back up mapping tables, so a restored or replicated metastore can rebuild identical policies; validate post-restore with deny tests.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Order filter logic cheap-to-expensive (group checks before subqueries), reference partition/clustering columns so file pruning still applies, keep mapping tables broadcastable, and avoid correlated subqueries that force per-row table scans by using EXISTS against a small indexed/clustered ACL.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: RLS eliminates duplicate per-tenant/per-region table copies and the redundant ETL to maintain them, trading a small per-query predicate cost for large savings in storage and pipeline compute; keep filters efficient so warehouses do not run longer.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Functions and mapping tables must be owned by a restricted security team and not modifiable by consumers; filters should fail closed (return FALSE for unknown principals); prefer account-level is_account_group_member over workspace-local is_member; never embed secrets, and ensure no alternate ungoverned path (e.g., direct cloud storage access) bypasses Unity Catalog.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use system.access.audit and query history to observe access patterns, and information_schema.row_filters/column_masks to verify bindings; alert on policy detachment, function ownership changes, or ACL edits outside the approved pipeline.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Maintain automated deny/allow tests: a synthetic unauthorized user must get zero rows and masked columns, an admin must see all rows; run these in CI before promoting schema or policy changes and after any metastore restore.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Centralize Unity Catalog audit logs, alert on ALTER TABLE DROP ROW FILTER/DROP MASK events, on changes to filter/mask function definitions, and on mass entitlement changes in the mapping table that could indicate misconfiguration or abuse.

recommendedPractices: **Prefer group-based checks:** Use is_account_group_member with identity-provider-synced groups instead of hardcoding user emails so policies survive personnel changes.
**Fail closed:** Design filter functions to return FALSE (deny) for principals not found in the mapping table, so gaps hide data rather than leak it.
**Combine filters with masks:** Use row filters for row visibility and column masks for cell-level redaction; do not overload one mechanism to do both.
**Keep mapping tables small and clustered:** Externalize entitlements into compact, broadcastable ACL tables and cluster protected tables on filter columns for pruning.
engineeringStandards: Filter and mask functions live in a dedicated, access-restricted governance schema owned by the security team.
All policy DDL (functions and ALTER TABLE bindings) is version-controlled and deployed via CI/CD, never edited ad hoc in production.
Every table classified as sensitive must have a verified row filter and required column masks before it can be granted to consumers.
designRecommendations: Branch cheap group checks before expensive mapping-table joins to short-circuit for privileged roles.
Reference partition/liquid-clustering columns inside filters so Databricks can prune files rather than scan everything.
Use EXISTS against a small clustered ACL for many-to-many entitlements instead of correlated scalar subqueries.
namingConventions: Name filter functions by the protected dimension, e.g., region_filter, tenant_filter, dept_filter.
Name mask functions mask_<column>, e.g., mask_email, mask_ssn; name ACL tables <entity>_acl or <dimension>_map.
documentationStandards: Document for each protected table which filter and masks are bound, the groups that bypass them, and the owning team.
Maintain a policy manifest mapping tables to their expected filters/masks for automated drift detection.
Record the business rule and compliance requirement (GDPR/HIPAA/SOC 2) each policy satisfies.
testingStrategies: Run allow/deny tests in CI impersonating representative groups: admin sees all, tenant user sees subset, unknown user sees none.
Assert masked columns return redacted values for non-privileged groups and raw values for privileged ones.
Test performance with realistic data volumes to confirm the filter still enables file pruning and does not regress query latency.

commonMistakes.mistake: Implementing RLS with proliferating secured views instead of native row filters.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Teams carry over pre-Unity-Catalog habits or are unaware that native row filters/column masks exist and are GA.
commonMistakes.impact: Dozens of nearly identical views drift apart, are easy to mis-grant, and create maintenance and audit nightmares.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: On Unity Catalog, attach a single row-filter function (and column masks) to the base table so all consumers inherit one centrally governed policy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Filter functions that fail open (return NULL/TRUE) for unknown users.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: A mapping-table lookup returns NULL when the user is absent and the logic treats that ambiguously, or a default branch returns TRUE.
commonMistakes.impact: Unauthorized or newly added users may see all rows, a direct data leak, exactly the failure RLS is meant to prevent.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Design filters to return FALSE by default; use EXISTS-style boolean logic so a missing entitlement deterministically denies access.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring performance: filters that block file pruning or do per-row table scans.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Filters reference non-clustered columns or use correlated scalar subqueries against large mapping tables.
commonMistakes.impact: Every query full-scans the protected table and re-runs an expensive subquery per row, sharply increasing latency and cost.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Reference partition/clustering columns, keep mapping tables small and broadcastable, and use EXISTS against clustered ACLs; check groups before subqueries.

comparisonSection.optionB: View-based RLS (secured views with WHERE clause)
comparisonSection.explanation: Row filters attach one reusable function to the base table so every consumer and tool inherits the policy automatically; view-based RLS requires creating and granting separate views, hiding base tables, and risks drift and inconsistent grants as the number of audiences grows.

Native row filters handle row visibility and separate column masks handle cell redaction, each independently testable and auditable; cramming both into a view's SELECT/WHERE couples concerns and makes the logic harder to reason about, though a view can also reshape schema which masks/filters alone cannot.

comparisonSection.optionA: Logical RLS on one shared table
comparisonSection.explanation: Logical RLS keeps a single governed copy with a query-time predicate (lower storage, easy onboarding) but adds per-query overhead; physical isolation gives the strongest blast-radius separation and simplest reasoning but multiplies storage, pipelines, and operational toil and is harder to query cross-tenant for internal analytics.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is Row Level Security in Databricks and how do you implement it?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Row Level Security restricts which rows a user can see in a table. In Databricks Unity Catalog you implement it by creating a SQL UDF that returns a boolean per row (the row filter) and binding it to a table with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER fn ON (col). Unity Catalog then applies the function as a predicate on every query for that table.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that it is a Unity Catalog feature, function-based, and applied transparently at query time rather than requiring users to add WHERE clauses.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between a row filter and a column mask?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A row filter decides which entire rows a principal can see by returning TRUE/FALSE per row. A column mask transforms or redacts the value of a specific column (e.g., showing only the last 4 digits) for unauthorized principals. A table can have one row filter but many column masks; the filter runs first, then masks redact surviving rows.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Show you understand both operate at query time via Unity Catalog functions and are complementary for full cell-level governance.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you implement group-based and multi-tenant RLS, and why use a mapping table?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use is_account_group_member('grp') for role-based bypass (e.g., admins see all) and a mapping/ACL table joined on current_user() for per-user entitlements. A mapping table externalizes the user-to-data relationship so you change access by editing data, not redeploying functions, and it supports many-to-many entitlements (one user, several tenants) via EXISTS.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Highlight account-group functions over workspace-local is_member, and the operational benefit of data-driven entitlements for multi-tenant SaaS.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do row filters affect query performance and how do you mitigate it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: The filter is injected as a predicate on every read, adding evaluation cost; mapping-table joins can be expensive and a poorly written filter may block file pruning. Mitigate by checking cheap group membership before subqueries, referencing partition/clustering columns so pruning still applies, keeping mapping tables small and broadcastable, and using EXISTS against a clustered ACL instead of correlated scalar subqueries.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate awareness of the plan rewrite and concrete optimization levers, not just that 'it adds overhead.'

advancedQuestions.question: Compare row-filter-based RLS to view-based RLS and to physical tenant isolation. When would you choose each?
advancedQuestions.answer: Row filters centralize one reusable policy on the base table with automatic inheritance and combine with column masks; choose them on Unity Catalog for many audiences over one governed copy. View-based RLS is needed when not on UC or when you also must reshape schema, but it causes view sprawl and grant drift. Physical isolation (table/partition per tenant) gives the strongest blast-radius separation and no query overhead but multiplies storage, ETL, and operational toil; choose it for the highest isolation/regulatory requirements or extreme latency needs.
advancedQuestions.explanation: A strong answer weighs governance simplicity, performance, blast radius, and operational cost rather than declaring one universally best.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you ensure a row filter cannot be bypassed and fails securely?
advancedQuestions.answer: Own filter/mask functions and mapping tables in a restricted governance schema so consumers cannot alter them; design filters to return FALSE for principals absent from the ACL (fail closed); use account-level group functions; ensure there is no ungoverned access path (e.g., direct cloud storage or Hive Metastore) that skips Unity Catalog; and audit bindings via information_schema with alerts on DROP ROW FILTER or function changes.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to hear least privilege, fail-closed design, no side channels, and continuous auditing, not just the happy-path DDL.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A multi-tenant SaaS keeps all customer events in one Delta table. Each customer must see only their rows, support engineers must see all tenants, and a user can belong to multiple tenants. Design the RLS.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Identify the protected dimension (tenant_id) and the bypass role (support group). Recognize many-to-many entitlement needs an ACL table and EXISTS. Decide enforcement at the base table for inheritance. Ensure fail-closed and pruning on tenant_id.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Create tenant_acl(user_email, tenant_id). Create tenant_filter(tenant_id) RETURN is_account_group_member('platform_support') OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tenant_acl WHERE user_email = current_user() AND tenant_id = tenant_filter.tenant_id). Bind it: ALTER TABLE events SET ROW FILTER tenant_filter ON (tenant_id). Cluster events on tenant_id, keep the ACL broadcastable, and add CI deny tests.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a governed lakehouse for a global company where regional analysts see only their region, HQ sees all, compensation columns are masked except for HR, and policies must be auditable and centrally managed.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use Unity Catalog with a governance schema. Create region_filter(region) branching on is_account_group_member('hq') else matching a region_map on current_user(). Create mask_comp(amount) returning raw value only for the 'hr' group. Bind the filter and mask to each fact table. Store all DDL in source control and deploy via CI/CD.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: One shared governed copy minimizes storage and view sprawl but adds per-query predicate cost; group-based logic is robust to personnel change but requires disciplined IdP group management; masks/filters cannot reshape schema, so genuinely different layouts still need views.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Keep region_map small and broadcastable, cluster fact tables on region for pruning, branch cheap group checks first, and monitor query latency. As tables grow, add automated drift detection via information_schema and alert on policy detachment; for extreme isolation needs of specific regulated datasets, fall back to physical isolation.

followUpQuestions: Can a table have more than one row filter? How do you express multiple conditions?
What is the difference between is_account_group_member and is_member, and which should you prefer?
How would you audit which tables currently have row filters and masks applied?
What happens to row filters when a cluster restarts or you query from a SQL warehouse vs a notebook?
How do you test that an RLS policy fails closed for an unknown user?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Row Level Security in Databricks binds a Unity Catalog boolean UDF (row filter) to a table so every query only returns rows the current principal is allowed to see, often combined with column masks.
keyConcepts: Row Filter: boolean UDF applied as a per-row predicate via ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER.
Column Mask: UDF that redacts a column value per principal; many allowed per table.
Mapping/ACL table: externalizes user-to-data entitlements for data-driven, multi-tenant RLS.
One row filter per table; runs before masks; enforced transparently across all compute.
commands: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sec.region_filter(region STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN RETURN is_account_group_member('admins') OR region = (SELECT r FROM sec.user_map WHERE u = current_user());
ALTER TABLE prod.sales SET ROW FILTER sec.region_filter ON (region);
ALTER TABLE prod.app.customers ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK sec.mask_email;
ALTER TABLE prod.sales DROP ROW FILTER;  ALTER TABLE prod.app.customers ALTER COLUMN email DROP MASK;
SELECT * FROM prod.information_schema.row_filters;  SELECT * FROM prod.information_schema.column_masks;
interviewPoints: Row filters are Unity Catalog functions bound to tables and applied transparently at query time.
Only one row filter per table; combine conditions inside it; many column masks allowed.
Design filters to fail closed; restrict ownership of functions and mapping tables.
Optimize by group-check-first, referencing clustering columns for pruning, and broadcastable ACLs.
quickNotes: RLS requires Unity Catalog; not available in legacy Hive Metastore.
Use mapping tables with EXISTS for many-to-many, multi-tenant entitlements.
Row filter eliminates rows before downstream operators; column masks redact surviving rows.
Audit bindings via information_schema.row_filters / column_masks and alert on DROP events.
Compared to view-based RLS, native filters avoid view sprawl and grant drift.

keyTakeaways: Databricks Row Level Security is implemented by binding a Unity Catalog boolean UDF (a row filter) to a table with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER, after which every query is transparently filtered to the rows the current principal may see.
A table can have exactly one row filter but many column masks; the filter eliminates rows first and masks then redact sensitive columns on the survivors, together giving full cell-level governance.

Group-based checks (is_account_group_member) plus a mapping/ACL table joined on current_user() deliver data-driven, multi-tenant isolation that you change by editing data rather than redeploying code, and should fail closed for unknown users.

Compared to view-based RLS, native row filters centralize one reusable policy on the base table with automatic inheritance, avoiding view sprawl and grant drift, while physical isolation remains the choice for maximum blast-radius separation.

Performance hinges on writing efficient filters: check cheap group membership first, reference partition/clustering columns to preserve file pruning, and keep mapping tables small and broadcastable to minimize per-query overhead.
